blocks.text: **The problem.** Given two words, return the fewest operations that turn `word1` into `word2`. Each operation **inserts**, **deletes** or **replaces** one letter.

blocks.alt: The DP table for horse down the side and ros along the top. Row 0 counts up 0, 1, 2, 3 and column 0 counts up 0 to 5: building from nothing or deleting everything. The bottom-right cell holds 3. Walking back from it: delete e, keep s, delete r, keep o, and replace h with r. So horse becomes rorse, then rose, then ros: three edits.

blocks.code:
word1 = "horse",      word2 = "ros"        ->  3   (replace h with r, delete r, delete e)
word1 = "intention",  word2 = "execution"  ->  5
word1 = "cat",        word2 = "cut"        ->  1   (replace a with u)

blocks.text: The idea: three moves at the last letter
Use the same table as Longest Common Subsequence: `dp[i][j]` is the fewest edits that turn the first i letters of `word1` into the first j letters of `word2`. Look at the last letter of each prefix.

If they're **equal**, they cost nothing: `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]`. If they **differ**, the last step of the best edit sequence is one of three moves, each leaving a smaller question: **replace** the letter (then turn i - 1 letters into j - 1: the diagonal), **delete** it (turn i - 1 letters into j: above), or **insert** `word2`'s letter (turn i letters into j - 1: left). Take 1 plus the cheapest. The edges are i deletes (column 0) and j inserts (row 0).
**Time O(3ⁿ⁺ᵐ) in the worst case, space O(n + m)** for the call stack. Every mismatch branches three ways, and the same `(i, j)` pairs come up again and again — a memo turns it into the table below.

blocks.caption: A matching letter copies the diagonal; otherwise take one edit plus the cheapest of replace, delete or insert.

blocks.text: **Time O(n · m), space O(n · m).** Walking back from the bottom-right cell — following whichever neighbour gave each value — lists one shortest sequence of edits, as the simulator's last step shows.
As with LCS, each row only needs the one above it. The one new detail: row 0 starts as `0, 1, 2, …` and each new row starts with `i`, the cost of deleting i letters.
**Time O(n · m), space O(m)** — or O(min(n, m)) by putting the shorter word along the rows, since the distance is the same in both directions.

blocks.alt: Plain recursion: O(3^(n+m)) time, O(n + m) space. Table: O(n·m) time, O(n·m) space. Two rows: O(n·m) time, O(m) space.

blocks.text: Edit distance is LCS with costs: the same table, the same last-letter reasoning, one more move. Spell checkers, DNA alignment and `diff` all run on this table.

items: **An empty word** — the answer is the other word's length: all inserts or all deletes.
**One letter different** — `"cat"` and `"cut"`: one replace, not a delete plus an insert.
**Very different lengths** — `"a"` and `"abcdef"`: the edge row and column carry most of the cost.
**Wrong edges** — row 0 and column 0 are `0, 1, 2, …`, not zeros: that's the difference from LCS.
**One Edit Distance** — are two strings exactly one edit apart? Two pointers in O(n), no table needed.
**Delete Operation for Two Strings** — only deletes allowed: n + m - 2 · LCS.
**Minimum ASCII Delete Sum** — deletes cost the letter's code: the same table with weighted moves.
**Longest Common Subsequence** — the same table, maximising shared letters instead of minimising edits. First lesson of this pattern.
